Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

crimlab 0.0.0.9000

  • relchk() recomputes a reported odds ratio, risk ratio or risk difference from its table under every labelling (each reference group, each outcome as the event, groups in rows or in columns) and says which readings reproduce the value as rounded: the labelling the report states, another one, or none. Zero cells give Inf or NaN, never a correction. proof("relchk") names the Lean theorems on how the contrasts change under relabelling.
  • catchk() audits categorical inputs before an analysis: storage type, levels and counts, missing values, unused and rare levels, labels that differ only by case or white space, 0/1 and logical codings, numbers that look like category codes, value labels that disagree with the values, and the reference level a default would take and why. It can check a stated reference level, and changes nothing.
  • Disparity tests: vodtst(), orrisk(), outtst(), dspbm(), dyadrt().
  • Forensic statistics: gtmp(), lrpost(), cllr(), cllrmin(), lrcal(), mixlr(), kinidx(), patidx(), dbsrch(), tipplt(), eceplt().
  • clrsmp() splits a change in a clearance rate into rate and mix effects and flags Simpson’s paradox.
  • expbnd() bounds rates and disparities when exposure is known only through a proxy.
  • misrd() gives the risk difference when group membership is misrecorded.
  • rtmhs() measures regression to the mean at selected hot spots.
  • incap() gives the crime rate and share prevented under incapacitation.
  • incapr() gives crimes prevented under desistance and replacement.
  • sellab() bounds the failure rate of a release rule from released defendants alone.
  • losbnd() bounds the mean time in custody from completed and open stays.
  • sntbnd() bounds the effect of a sentence on a binary outcome without assumptions.
  • hzdsel() shows how period-two hazards differ after selective depletion.
  • Networks: coofg() builds the co-offending graph of an incident table; ntdeg(), ntbtw(), ntcls() and ntevc() give degree, betweenness, closeness and eigenvector centrality; ntcore() cores, ntcmp() components, ntlvn() and ntmod() Louvain communities and modularity, ntbrk() Gould-Fernandez brokerage and ntchg() the Cheeger bounds. Results are by node label in order of first appearance.
  • Spatial: hvdist() and eqproj()/eqinv() for longitude and latitude; cgstat(), cgmedn(), webpt(), sdell() and cvhull() for centres, spread and hulls; nnidx(), ripk() and ripenv() for nearest neighbours and K functions; fzmode(), kmpart(), nnhclu() and stacel() for hot spots; mantst() and stmavg() in space and time; jtdecay(), jtsurf(), jtcal(), jtacc() and bjtc() for journey to crime. Points come as vectors, tables or sf points; longitude and latitude only with lonlat = TRUE.
  • Spatial weights and autocorrelation: spwt() (k nearest, distance band, contiguity; binary or inverse distance), gearc() (Geary’s C), gorg() (the Getis-Ord G), lmorn() (local Moran with conditional permutations), locgi() (local G and G*) and dirmn() (directional mean).
  • fair() (fairness of a risk tool by group), tlvc() and tlvlr() (trace evidence), aorwt() (aoristic weights), bdig() and bnft() (Benford screens), skp() (Scott-Knott grouping), rptc() (constant reporters), rswp() and rshl() (Rosenbaum bounds), zgll(), zgem(), mvtll() and mvtem() (group-based trajectories), tfrp() (glass transfer), lwss() (lowess), chmb() (tool marks), gstr() (grid Gi*) and sptst() (Andresen’s point pattern test).
  • proof() names the Lean theorem behind each function; the proofs ship in inst/lean.
  • A vector longer than the largest integer is refused with an error, by the exported functions and by the compiled entry points alike; the compiled code used to truncate its length.
  • eceplt() gives the calibrated curve its limits at extreme prior odds: a calibrated ratio of 0 or infinity used to give NaN, or an error.
  • incapr() refuses a t0 + s beyond the length of lam however large the two are; past the largest integer it used to warn of an integer overflow and stop with an unrelated error.
  • sntbnd() orders the two values of z by Unicode code point, so the default treat and the order of the terms are the same on every machine and in every locale ("B" sorts before "a").
  • Every error message starts with the name of the function that raised it ("outtst: `q` must be at most 1."); the words after it are unchanged.
  • A matrix with more than one row and column is refused where a vector is expected, naming the argument; it used to be read as one long vector.
  • eceplt() labels its vertical axis in bits.
  • proof() names the theorems now proved for gtmp(), cllr(), dbsrch(), mixlr(), kinidx(), patidx(), misrd(), incap(), lrcal() and cllrmin(). The help pages of misrd(), cllr() and cllrmin() say what is proved and what is not.
  • vignette("crimlab") walks through one example per family.
  • Arguments that hold one value per group are matched by name. Named inputs whose names come in another order were read by position, a wrong answer: vodtst(c(white = 600, black = 400), c(black = 300, white = 700)) read 300 as the white night count. Now every later argument is put in the order of the first by name; names that differ, or a name given twice, are an error that lists them. Unnamed inputs are still matched by position. This holds in vodtst(), dspbm(), dyadrt() (the row and column names of count too), clrsmp(), expbnd(), incap(), gtmp(), hzdsel(), and for loci in kinidx() and patidx(); per-unit arguments of outtst(), rtmhs(), lrpost(), sellab() and sntbnd() are matched by name when every one has unique names.
  • Per-group arguments also accept a list of single numbers and a one-row data frame; a one-row or one-column matrix gives its names.
  • vodtst() takes one table of groups by day and night (a matrix, 2-d table or data frame with columns named day and night) with night left out.
  • vodtst(), dspbm() and expbnd() return a ref column marking the reference group; a factor ref is read by its label.
  • sntbnd() no longer picks the treatment by sorting the values of z: treat is required unless z is logical (TRUE is the treatment) or 0 and 1 (1 is).
  • A labelled vector (with a labels attribute, as haven makes) is refused with a request to decode it first: its numbers are category codes.
  • Learning: enpath(), the elastic net path by coordinate descent with cross-validation over given folds (the objective and scale of glmnet); lgtreg(), logistic regression; rfor(), random forests for regression and probabilities.
  • Causal estimates: dmlx(), double machine learning by cross-fitting for the partially linear, interactive, IV, difference-in-differences and sample-selection models, with AIPW and TMLE from the same nuisances.

Developed by Vansh Singh Ruhela.
